newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Ranariddh denies Khmer Rouge alliance.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Ranariddh denies Khmer Rouge alliance.

text.p: The Khmer Rouge guerrilla group said on Friday it had joined forces with Prince Norodom Ranariddh's senior military commander to fight Cambodia's powerful leader Hun Sen, a claim the ousted co-prime minister promptly denied.

In the Khmer Rouge report on their clandestine radio, the long-time propaganda mouthpiece of the Maoist movement, the rebels said current and former Khmer Rouge guerrillas had formed a joint military command with royalists fighting government troops in the northwest of the country.
"On August 13, 1997, the national resistance forces...designated a joint general staff to fight the (Vietnamese) communists and their puppet Hun Sen," said the radio report monitored in Phnom Penh.
It said the alliance included General Nhiek Bun Chhay, Ranariddh's senior military commander, and Ei Chien, the former Khmer Rouge commander who defected to the government last year.

Ranariddh, whose premiership was wrested away by Hun Sen last month, denied forming any military or political alliance with the rebels, although some of his forces in Cambodia's northwest have said they were fighting alongside the rebels.
"There is no alliance with the Khmer Rouge, either political or military," he told reporters in Bangkok.

When asked if Nhiek Bun Chhay could have made a deal with the rebels without his knowledge, Ranariddh said, "I don't know, I have to check. But Nhiek Bun Chhay could not do anything without my approval."

Ranariddh's rag-tag forces have been fighting the government in the northwest since the prince and his royalist forces were overthrown by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, his coalition government partner, on July 6.
The Khmer Rouge have condemned the coup and broadcast frequent verbal attacks on Hun Sen, who was with the Vietnamese forces that invaded Cambodia in 1978 and toppled the Khmer Rouge regime.
Ranariddh was negotiating with the rebels for several months and reportedly reached an alliance with them just before Hun Sen's July power grab.
Late last month, the guerrillas purged their infamous leader, Pol Pot, in an apparent effort to sanitise their image and any alliance with Ranariddh.
The United States has condemned any future political role for the Khmer Rouge, under whose 1975-79 rule more than a million Cambodians died of overwork, torture, execution, starvation or disease.
Ranariddh, eager to court international support, has said in the past he will not cooperate with the rebels.
But royalist troops said on Thursday they were fighting alongside Khmer Rouge rebels in O'Smach, the last major town held by opposition forces.
Hun Sen's forces have pressed closer to O'Smach in recent days and on Thursday heordered his army to seize O'Smach immediately.

A fighting alliance between royalists and Khmer Rouge would mirror their partnership in the 1980s, when they were part of an opposition fighting a Vietnamese occupation forces and Hun Sen's Hanoi-backed government.

The rebels signed a peace agreement in 1991 that paved the way for U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993, but later reneged on the deal and waged a low-intensity guerrilla war against the coalition government that emerged from the poll.
Hun Sen and Ung Huot, Ranariddh's replacement as first prime minister, flew to Beijing this week to seek the blessing of Ranariddh's father, King Norodom Sihanouk, for the new government.
Ung Huot told reporters on his return to Phnom Penh that they had won endorsement from Sihanouk, who is in Beijing receiving medical treatment.
Sihanouk later said he had not given his blessing and that, by law, Ranariddh was still co-premier with Hun Sen.
